objectives: Read an HR diagram and identify the four main regions.
Predict a star's main-sequence lifetime from its mass.
Trace post-main-sequence evolution by initial mass.

slides.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram
slides.body:
**HR diagram**: temperature (or spectral type) on the x-axis (reversed: hot left), luminosity on the y-axis (log). When Hertzsprung (1911) and Russell (1913) plotted nearby stars, they didn't fill the diagram uniformly — stars **cluster** in four bands:

1. **Main sequence**: diagonal band from top-left (hot, luminous, massive O stars) to bottom-right (cool, faint, low-mass M dwarfs). ~90% of stars at any moment. They're H-burning.
2. **Red giants**: cool (3000-5000 K) but luminous (10² - 10³ L☉) — upper right. Post-MS, He-burning or shell-H-burning stars.
3. **Supergiants**: very cool and extremely luminous (10⁴ - 10⁶ L☉) — top right. Massive stars near death (Betelgeuse, Antares).
4. **White dwarfs**: hot (8000-100000 K) but very faint (10⁻² - 10⁻⁴ L☉) — bottom left. Earth-sized degenerate stellar corpses.

The MS is *not* an evolutionary track — each star sits at one point on it for most of its life, then leaves rapidly.

slides.title: Mass-luminosity-lifetime scalings
slides.body:
On the main sequence, three empirical/theoretical scalings:

• **L ~ M^3.5** (between ~0.5 and 50 M☉). Steeper at low mass, shallower at high mass.
• **R ~ M^0.8** (rough — depends on regime).
• **T_eff ~ M^0.5** (combining L=4πR²σT⁴ with the above).

Main-sequence lifetime **t_MS ~ M/L ~ M^−2.5**:
- Sun (M=1): ~10 Gyr.
- 10 M☉: ~30 Myr.
- 50 M☉: ~5 Myr.
- 0.5 M☉ (red dwarf): ~50-200 Gyr (longer than the age of the universe!).

The HR diagram is a snapshot — what you observe is the **age-distribution-weighted superposition** of every burning star. Bright O stars are rare because they're short-lived; M dwarfs are most numerous (~75% of all stars) because they live forever.

slides.title: Post-main-sequence: the off-ramp
slides.body:
When core H runs out, the star leaves the MS. Trajectories depend almost entirely on **initial mass**:

• **M < 0.5 M☉**: never ignites He → cools into a **He white dwarf** (universe isn't old enough for this to have happened yet — projected).
• **0.5 < M < 8 M☉**: red giant branch (H-shell burning) → He flash (degenerate He core ignites) → horizontal branch (core He) → asymptotic giant branch (He + H shells) → planetary nebula → **C/O white dwarf**. Sun follows this.
• **8 < M < 25 M☉**: blue/red supergiants → onion-shell burning (H, He, C, Ne, O, Si) → iron core → **core-collapse supernova (Type II)** → **neutron star**.
• **25 < M < 100 M☉**: similar but more mass loss + larger Fe core → **black hole**.
• **M > ~140 M☉**: pair-instability supernova — total disruption, no remnant. Rare; likely some Population III stars.

White dwarfs respect the **Chandrasekhar limit** (1.4 M☉) — above this, electron degeneracy can't hold against gravity → collapse to NS or BH.

slides.title: Predict the lifetime of Sirius A
slides.statement: Sirius A is a main-sequence A1V star with mass ≈ 2.06 M☉ and luminosity ≈ 25 L☉. Estimate its MS lifetime and compare to the Sun.

steps.prompt: Use t_MS = 10 Gyr × (M/L) (in solar units) — the same energy budget but adjusted for luminosity. What's the value?
steps.hint: More fuel ⇒ longer life, but burning faster ⇒ shorter — M/L is the ratio.

steps.prompt: Use the simpler t_MS ~ M^−2.5 scaling. Does it agree?
steps.answer: t_MS ≈ 10 Gyr × (2.06)^(−2.5) ≈ 10 × 0.165 ≈ 1.65 Gyr. Roughly within factor 2 of the M/L estimate. The discrepancy reflects that the L-M relation isn't a perfect M^3.5 (it's shallower for A-type stars).

steps.prompt: Sirius is ~250 Myr old. Roughly what fraction of its MS lifetime has elapsed?
steps.answer: Using t_MS ≈ 1 Gyr (geometric mean of the two estimates): about 25-30%. So Sirius A is comfortably middle-aged on the MS.

steps.prompt: Sirius B is a white dwarf companion to Sirius A. What does this tell us about Sirius B's initial mass?
steps.answer: Sirius B has already finished its MS life — so its progenitor was more massive than Sirius A (more massive ⇒ shorter life). Estimates put the progenitor at ~5 M☉. Stellar evolution explains why the more massive star is now a corpse while the less massive star is still on the MS.
steps.hint: The white dwarf is older — what was its progenitor mass?

slides.prompt: Why do most stars in a globular cluster sit on the lower main sequence and the red-giant branch, with no upper-main-sequence stars?

choices.label: Globular clusters preferentially form low-mass stars (IMF is bottom-heavy).
choices.rationale: The IMF (initial mass function, Salpeter dN/dM ∝ M^−2.35) is similar across environments. The reason isn't formation — it's evolution.

choices.label: Massive stars in globular clusters have already evolved off the MS and become white dwarfs / neutron stars / black holes.
choices.rationale: Correct. Globular clusters are ~12 Gyr old. Any star with t_MS < 12 Gyr (i.e., M > ~0.9 M☉) has finished its main-sequence life and moved on. What you see is everything with M ≤ 0.9 M☉ still on the MS, plus the red-giant remnants of slightly more massive stars currently in their (much shorter) post-MS phases.

choices.label: Massive stars have been ejected by dynamical interactions in the dense cluster core.
choices.rationale: Mass segregation in dense clusters tends to sink (not eject) massive stars to the center. Some ejection happens, but it doesn't explain the systematic absence of upper-MS stars.

choices.label: Globular cluster stars are too metal-poor to support CNO burning, so massive stars can't form.
choices.rationale: Low metallicity affects opacity + the upper IMF slightly, but Population II stars routinely form massive stars (now observed in earliest-universe galaxies). The 'missing' upper-MS in modern observations is purely an age effect.

slides.hint: Globular clusters are old. Use t_MS ~ M^−2.5 to find the turnoff mass.
slides.workedSolution: For t_MS = 12 Gyr: M = (10/12)^(1/2.5) ≈ 0.93 M☉. So everything more massive than 0.93 M☉ has already left the MS, and the cluster's HR diagram shows a sharp **turnoff** at that mass. The turnoff luminosity is a clock — older cluster ⇒ lower turnoff. This is how globular-cluster ages were derived before Gaia parallaxes.

slides.prompt: You observe a star with T_eff = 4000 K and L = 200 L☉. Use the HR diagram to identify it.

choices.label: Main-sequence K dwarf.
choices.rationale: K dwarfs are bottom-right of the MS — cool but faint (L ≈ 0.1 - 0.5 L☉). 200 L☉ is two orders of magnitude too bright.

choices.label: Red giant.
choices.rationale: Yes. T_eff = 4000 K is cool, and L = 200 L☉ is 200× solar — this is the upper red-giant branch (RGB) or asymptotic giant branch (AGB) of a Sun-like (~1-2 M☉) star that has finished core H-burning. Typical examples: Aldebaran (Tau Tauri), Arcturus.

choices.label: Red supergiant.
choices.rationale: Supergiants are far brighter (L > 10⁴ L☉) — Betelgeuse is ~10⁵ L☉. 200 L☉ is too modest for a supergiant.

choices.label: White dwarf.
choices.rationale: White dwarfs have L < 0.1 L☉ and live in the bottom-left (cooler ones drift right as they age). They're certainly not at 200 L☉.

slides.hint: Place (T_eff, L) on the diagram and check which region matches.
slides.workedSolution: T_eff = 4000 K plots near the M/K boundary (right side of HR diagram). L = 200 L☉ ⇒ log L ≈ 2.3 ⇒ that's well above the main sequence (where a K star would be ~0.2 L☉). The point lands squarely in the red giant region. Approximate radius: R/R☉ = √(L/L☉)·(T☉/T)² ≈ √200 × (5780/4000)² ≈ 14 × 2.1 ≈ 30 R☉ — a typical red giant.

slides.prompt: A 5 M☉ main-sequence star has approximately what MS lifetime in Myr? Use t_MS ≈ 10 Gyr × M^−2.5 (M in solar units).
slides.workedSolution: 5^2.5 = 5²·√5 = 25·2.236 ≈ 55.9. So t_MS = 10000 / 55.9 ≈ 179 Myr. A 5-M☉ B-type star lives ~180 Myr — short enough that the OB associations we see in spiral arms are kinematic snapshots of recent star formation, not steady states.

slides.prompt: Explain in ≤120 words why the HR diagram is the single most important plot in astronomy — what does each axis encode, and what physics can you extract from a single point?
rubric: X-axis: T_eff (or color, or spectral type) ⇒ surface temperature ⇒ peak Wien wavelength, ionization state, dominant absorption lines.
Y-axis: luminosity (often absolute magnitude) ⇒ total power output.
From L + T_eff: R via Stefan-Boltzmann L = 4πR²σT⁴ ⇒ stellar radius without resolving the disk.
From the MS location: stellar mass via empirical L-M relation ⇒ then t_MS via M^-2.5.
From post-MS branch position: evolutionary phase (RGB, HB, AGB).
In one plot: temperature, luminosity, radius, mass, age, evolutionary phase. No other single diagnostic combines that much physics.
